# A Cluster-Randomised Trial of a 30-Hour Week in Municipal Administration: Nine-Month Results

*Varden County Evaluation Unit, in collaboration with the Department of Labour Economics, Easterly University. A. Lindqvist, P. Mahony and D. Rao. Registered protocol VC-2023-04.*

## Summary

We randomly assigned 24 administrative offices of a county government, employing 1,180 staff, to either reduce scheduled hours from 37.5 to 30 per week at full pay (12 offices) or continue on the standard schedule (12 offices) for nine months. Output was measured from administrative records, not from manager assessments, and actual hours from timesheets. The effect differed sharply by type of work. In case-processing offices, where work arrives as a backlog that can be cleared at any time, output per full-time employee changed by −2.1% (95% CI −6.8 to +2.6) relative to control and output per actual hour rose by 12.5%. In counter and contact-centre offices, where output depends on staff being present while the public is waiting, output per employee fell by 11.4% (95% CI −16.9 to −5.9), waiting times rose, and output per actual hour rose by a more modest 6.7%. Sick days fell by 29% across treated offices. An exploratory analysis suggests that a reduction in recurring meetings may account for part of the gain in case-processing offices.

## Motivation

Existing evidence on reduced working time comes mainly from voluntary pilots without comparison groups, in which output is often reported by the managers who sponsored the change. The county wished to know whether a reduced schedule could be extended to its own administrative staff without loss of service, and agreed to a randomised design with administrative output measures and a registered analysis plan.

## Design

**Units and randomisation.** The 24 offices were stratified into two strata by type of work before randomisation, and offices were randomised within strata:

- *Case-processing offices* (14 offices; 7 treated, 7 control): permits, licensing, benefits assessment and records. Work arrives as cases that join a queue and can be completed at any point within statutory deadlines.
- *Counter and contact-centre offices* (10 offices; 5 treated, 5 control): in-person service counters and telephone lines. Work arrives as members of the public who must be served while they wait.

Randomisation was at office level to avoid contamination between colleagues. Treated offices kept their public opening hours unchanged; staff rotas were rearranged so that each employee worked 30 scheduled hours.

**Outcomes.** The registered primary outcome is output per full-time-equivalent employee (FTE), measured as cases closed (case-processing) or contacts handled (counter and contact centre), from the county's case-management and telephony systems. Registered secondary outcomes are output per actual hour (from timesheets, which include any overtime claimed), quality (the share of decisions overturned on appeal; for contact centres, the repeat-contact rate within seven days), average waiting time, and sick days. Analysis is difference-in-differences against the six-month pre-period, with standard errors clustered by office.

**Exploratory measures.** At the request of office managers we also collected calendar data on recurring meetings in month six. This was not part of the registered plan.

## Results

### Hours

Scheduled hours fell by 20% in treated offices. Actual hours, from timesheets, fell by less: by 13% in case-processing offices (from 37.9 to 33.0 per week) and by 17% in counter offices (from 37.6 to 31.2), the difference reflecting overtime claimed to clear backlogs in case-processing. Control offices' actual hours were stable.

### Output and quality

**Table 1. Difference-in-differences estimates at nine months, treated relative to control**

| Outcome | Case-processing (7 v 7 offices) | Counter and contact centre (5 v 5 offices) |
|---|---|---|
| Output per FTE | −2.1% (−6.8 to +2.6) | −11.4% (−16.9 to −5.9) |
| Actual hours per FTE | −13% | −17% |
| Output per actual hour | +12.5% (+6.9 to +18.4) | +6.7% (+0.4 to +13.3) |
| Appeal overturn rate / repeat contact rate | 3.1% v 3.0% | 11.8% v 10.9% |
| Average wait (minutes), treated offices, pre → month 9 | — | 4.2 → 6.9 |
| Sick days per FTE | −29% (both strata pooled) | |

In case-processing offices, output per employee was statistically indistinguishable from control, with a point estimate slightly below zero, and quality was unchanged. Because actual hours fell by 13%, output per actual hour rose by 12.5%. Measured against scheduled rather than actual hours, the gain would appear as 22%; we regard that figure as misleading, because staff did not in fact work only the scheduled hours.

In counter and contact-centre offices, the picture is different. With the same number of staff each working fewer hours, fewer staff were present at any given time during unchanged opening hours. Contacts handled per employee fell by 11.4% and the average wait rose from 4.2 to 6.9 minutes. Output per actual hour rose by 6.7%, but this did not offset the loss of hours, and the service the public received was worse. Abandoned calls rose from 6% to 10% of calls.

### Wellbeing

Sick days fell by 29% in treated offices relative to control. Resignations were lower in treated offices (annualised 3.9% against 7.4%), though with 12 offices per arm and few resignations the estimate is imprecise.

### Exploratory: meetings

Calendar data in month six showed that staff in treated case-processing offices spent 3.8 hours per week in recurring meetings against 7.1 hours in control case-processing offices, a difference of 3.3 hours. Offices that cut meetings most showed the largest gains in output per hour (correlation across the 7 treated offices, r = 0.71). Interviews suggested that the reduced schedule prompted managers to cancel standing meetings that had persisted by habit.

We emphasise that this analysis was not registered, that it rests on seven offices, and that a correlation across seven offices cannot establish a mechanism. We report it because, if confirmed, it would mean that a substantial part of the per-hour gain comes from removing low-value time rather than from rest alone, and that would matter for how the result is interpreted and for what other employers could expect. We have registered a confirmatory test for the 24-month follow-up.

## Discussion

Three conclusions follow from the registered analyses.

First, in work where output is not tied to presence, a 20% cut in scheduled hours produced a much smaller cut in actual hours and little or no measurable loss of output per employee. Output per hour rose by about an eighth.

Second, in work where output is tied to presence, the same change reduced output per employee by about a tenth and worsened service, even though each hour worked was somewhat more productive. Gains per hour do not by themselves imply that the hours reduction pays for itself. The question "does a shorter week raise productivity?" therefore has at least two answers depending on whether productivity is understood per hour or per employee, and these come apart most sharply in coverage-bound work.

Third, estimates computed against scheduled hours materially overstate the per-hour gain. In our data the overstatement is from 12.5% to 22% in case-processing offices.

These findings qualify claims, made on the basis of uncontrolled pilots, that reduced hours are sector-general. A sector may contain both kinds of work; what matters is whether output in a given role depends on hours of presence.

## Limitations

The trial is in one public employer, with 24 offices; confidence intervals are correspondingly wide, particularly in the counter stratum. Staff knew their assignment, and control staff knew that a trial was under way, which could have affected effort in either direction. Nine months may be too short to reveal whether gains persist after the novelty of the change wears off, or whether backlogs build up beyond the statutory deadlines. Public-sector case processing may differ from private-sector knowledge work in ways that affect the result. A 24-month follow-up is under way.

response:
# Review: *A Cluster-Randomised Trial of a 30-Hour Week in Municipal Administration* (Varden County)

This is a much stronger study than the Halden pilot. It addresses that paper's main weaknesses one by one: it has a randomised control group, output comes from administrative records, actual hours come from timesheets, the analysis was registered, randomisation was stratified by type of work, and the exploratory analysis is clearly labelled. The Discussion is appropriately restrained.

The core arithmetic checks out:

- **Hours:** 37.9 → 33.0 is −12.9%, and 37.6 → 31.2 is −17.0%.
- **Output per actual hour:** 0.979 / 0.87 = +12.5%, and 0.886 / 0.83 = +6.7%.
- **Scheduled-hours comparison:** 0.979 / 0.8 = +22.4%, matching the "22%" figure.

What follows are mostly gaps in reporting and inference, plus two points that change how the results should be read.

---

## 1. Points that affect interpretation

**1a. The per-hour gain in counter offices is probably queueing, not efficiency.**
In coverage-bound work, demand arrives regardless of staffing. With fewer staff present, each one has less idle time between customers. Output per hour therefore rises because utilisation rises, and the same thing makes waits longer and calls get abandoned. The +6.7% is best read as lost slack, not as staff working more effectively. The Discussion presents it as "each hour worked was somewhat more productive." It should either reframe the figure or show that the gain holds when demand is held fixed, for example at times of day with comparable queue lengths.

**1b. Some of the counter offices' output may be repeat demand.**
The repeat-contact rate is higher in treated offices (11.8% vs 10.9%), and repeat contacts count as output. Some contacts handled are therefore re-handling of earlier failures. The text says nothing about this. It only reports that quality was unchanged in *case-processing* offices. Counter-office quality appears to have worsened, and the paper should say so.

**1c. Contamination through shared systems.**
If county telephone lines route overflow calls between contact centres, or if cases can be reassigned between offices, then treated offices' unmet demand may have flowed to control offices. That would inflate control output and exaggerate the treated–control gap, or the reverse depending on how output is attributed. The paper should state whether routing or case reassignment crosses offices. For counter offices this is a real risk, not a theoretical one.

**1d. Overtime cost is never mentioned.**
In case-processing offices, actual hours of 33.0 against 30 scheduled means about 3 hours per week of claimed overtime per FTE. That overtime is presumably paid on top of full pay, likely at a premium rate. Output per FTE was roughly unchanged, so cost per case closed rose. For a county deciding whether to extend the schedule, cost per case is arguably the most relevant outcome. It should be reported.

---

## 2. Statistical inference

**2a. Too few clusters for standard clustered errors.**
The comparisons rest on 7 v 7 and 5 v 5 offices. Conventional cluster-robust standard errors are known to understate uncertainty at these sample sizes. Report wild-cluster-bootstrap or randomisation-inference p-values as a sensitivity check. The counter per-hour interval (+0.4 to +13.3) barely excludes zero and may not survive the correction.

**2b. No formal test that the strata differ.**
The headline is that "the effect differed sharply by type of work." The paper reports two separate intervals but no test of the difference between them. My rough estimate from the reported intervals gives a difference of about 9 points, SE ≈ 3.7, p ≈ 0.01, so the claim probably holds. Still, the interaction estimate should be reported, and the paper should state whether it was registered. Strata were defined before randomisation, which helps.

**2c. Table 1 mixes estimate types under a "difference-in-differences" heading.**
- The quality row gives raw treated-v-control levels ("3.1% v 3.0%"). It is unlabelled and has no interval.
- Waiting time is a treated-only before/after comparison with no control comparison, although it is a registered secondary outcome.
- Sick days are pooled across strata with no interval, even though everything else is stratified.
- Abandoned calls appear in the text but are not a registered outcome. They should be marked as such.
- Resignations (3.9% v 7.4%) are a post-period comparison, not a DiD, and have no interval.

Each row should be a DiD estimate with an interval, and anything that isn't should be labelled.

**2d. Parallel trends.**
The six-month pre-period allows a pre-trend check. Show it, even briefly. Randomisation makes problems unlikely, but with 5 offices per arm, chance imbalance is possible.

---

## 3. Missing outcomes

**Case-processing backlog and deadline compliance.**
The Limitations section raises the risk of "backlogs build[ing] up beyond the statutory deadlines," yet the paper reports neither. If cases arriving stayed constant and closures fell 2.1%, the backlog grew. Queue size, median time to decision and the share of cases decided within the statutory deadline are all available from the case-management system, and they are the case-processing counterpart to counter waiting times.

**Appeal lag.**
Appeals take time to resolve, so overturn rates at nine months mostly reflect decisions made early in the trial. Note this, and revisit the rate at 24 months.

**Sick days: days or hours?**
If the 30-hour week was delivered as fewer days rather than shorter days, part of the 29% drop is mechanical, because there are fewer scheduled days on which to be absent. The paper should state how rotas were structured and whether sick time was measured in days or hours.

**Distribution of staff.**
The paper doesn't say how the 1,180 staff split between strata and arms.

---

## 4. The exploratory meetings analysis

The paper is admirably candid about this analysis's limits. There are also two specific problems.

**"Offices that cut meetings most" can't be measured.**
Calendar data were collected only in month six, so there is no baseline from which to measure a cut. The correlation is between the *level* of meetings at month six and the per-hour gain. Randomisation makes it plausible that the 3.3-hour gap between arms was caused by the treatment, but office-level reductions are not observed. Rephrase accordingly.

**r = 0.71 across 7 offices is not statistically significant.**
It gives p ≈ 0.07, two-sided. Since the paper already disclaims the result, stating the p-value would reinforce that caution.

**Part of the link may be mechanical.**
If meeting time counts as hours worked but produces no cases, removing meetings raises output per hour by construction. That still matters, because it supports the authors' reading that low-value time was removed. But it means the meetings result is partly an accounting identity rather than independent evidence of a mechanism.

The registered confirmatory test at 24 months is the right response. Collect baseline calendar data for it if any can be recovered retrospectively.

---

## 5. Minor points

- The Summary mentions waiting times rising in counter offices but not the rise in abandoned calls (6% → 10%), which is arguably the more striking service result.
- "Staff knew … control staff knew that a trial was under way" could bias results in either direction: control staff might work harder or might become demoralised. Report any control-office change in output or sickness relative to their own pre-period.
- "Timesheets, which include any overtime claimed" means unclaimed extra work is invisible. Actual hours may therefore be understated, and the per-hour gain overstated. Mention this in Limitations.

---

## Overall

The design is sound and the main conclusions are supported:

- per-hour and per-employee productivity come apart;
- coverage-bound work bears the cost;
- scheduled-hours denominators overstate the gain, here from 12.5% to 22%.

The main improvements needed are:

1. Reframe the counter offices' per-hour gain as higher utilisation.
2. Rule out contamination through call and case routing.
3. Report cost per case, backlog and deadline compliance.
4. Use small-cluster-robust inference and test the interaction between strata formally.

Compared with the Halden working paper, this trial directly undercuts that paper's "sector-general" conclusion. It is a fair, well-designed test of the claim, and its result is the opposite.
